verses.text: Therefore seeing we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we faint not;

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God.
But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost:
In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them.
For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus’ sake.
For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair;
Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed;
Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body.
For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh.
So then death worketh in us, but life in you.
We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak;
Knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you.
For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God.
For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory;
While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.

chapters.summary: The chapter opens by drawing a conclusion from the glorious ministry just described, and the conclusion is endurance grounded in something other than stamina: "Therefore seeing we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we faint not." Paul then defines that ministry first by what he has refused — he has "renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully" — and then by his one permitted method, "by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God." No technique is left; only the truth set plainly before another person's conscience, with God watching. That confession forces him to account for failure without blaming his own methods: "But if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not, lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them." The obstacle is neither the message's obscurity nor the preacher's incompetence but an active hostile blinding, which is also why the preacher must be careful never to occupy the frame: "For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus’ sake." What breaks the blindness is a second act of creation, described in the language of the first: "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." Against that blaze Paul immediately sets the fragility of the people carrying it — "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" — and the reason is stated as purpose, not accident: the cheapness of the container is what makes the source of the power unmistakable. Four antitheses then trace the cracks in the vessel and the treasure holding it together: "We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; Persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed." Paul reads his own battered body as an exhibition of the Passion and the Resurrection at once, "Always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body," and repeats it to be sure it is not missed: "For we which live are alway delivered unto death for Jesus’ sake, that the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our mortal flesh." The exchange is then stated with unnerving brevity — "So then death worketh in us, but life in you" — an apostolic ministry that costs the minister and pays the church. Speech continues because faith does, and Paul claims continuity with the psalmist: "We having the same spirit of faith, according as it is written, I believed, and therefore have I spoken; we also believe, and therefore speak." The content of that faith is resurrection and reunion, "Knowing that he which raised up the Lord Jesus shall raise up us also by Jesus, and shall present us with you," and its purpose runs outward and then upward, "For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God." The chapter closes by repeating its opening refusal and explaining it: "For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day." Two things are happening in the same body at the same time, one visible decay and one invisible renewal, and the weighing of them yields the chapter's most audacious sentence: "For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory." This is possible only under a particular discipline of attention, which the final verse names: "While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal."
takeaways: "We faint not" frames the chapter twice, at verse one and again at verse sixteen, and each time Paul gives a reason that has nothing to do with his own resilience. The first is backward-looking — "as we have received mercy" — and the second is forward-looking, the eternal weight of glory being produced. Between those two bookends stands a catalogue of trouble, perplexity, persecution, and being cast down, so the refusal to faint is plainly not a claim to feel fine. Paul is perplexed; he simply is not in despair. The chapter therefore separates endurance from emotional buoyancy: what keeps the minister going is mercy already received and glory already guaranteed, neither of which fluctuates with how the week has gone.

The ministry Paul describes has been stripped of every instrument except transparency. He has "renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully," which rules out not only lying but the subtler professional arts — the managed impression, the selectively edited message, the text bent toward the effect one wants. What remains is "by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God," an appeal aimed at the hearer's conscience rather than at his admiration, and audited by God rather than by results. It is a deliberately defenseless way to work, and the rest of the chapter explains why a man who has renounced all leverage does not thereby become desperate.

Verses three and four remove a temptation that haunts anyone whose message is refused: the assumption that rejection is a verdict on the presentation. "If our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost: In whom the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not." The hiding is not in the gospel, which by definition is a manifestation, and not in Paul, who has just renounced craftiness; it is an active blinding with a stated aim, "lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them." Unbelief is here treated as something inflicted as well as chosen, which both dignifies the unbeliever's condition as a genuine bondage and removes the preacher's power to fix it by cleverness.

The remedy Paul names for that blindness is not argument but creation. "For God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts, to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ." The allusion is to the first day of the world, and the parallel is exact in its unilaterality: darkness contributes nothing to the arrival of light, and the same God who spoke then speaks now. Two further things follow from the verse's wording. The light is given as knowledge, not as sensation — it illuminates rather than merely warms — and its location is a human face, so that the glory once sought on a mountain or behind a veil is now met in a person.

"But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" is a statement of design, not of regret. Paul does not apologize for the pottery or promise that it will improve; the fragility is the point, because a container this obviously cheap makes it impossible to confuse the shine with the shell. The four antitheses that follow keep the same structure — troubled but not distressed, perplexed but not in despair, persecuted but not forsaken, cast down but not destroyed — and each pairs a real, unminimized affliction with a limit it cannot cross. The vessel is genuinely cracking, and every crack is where the argument for God's power is actually made.

The most confronting sentence in the chapter is its shortest: "So then death worketh in us, but life in you." Paul has just described himself as "always bearing about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus" so that "the life also of Jesus might be made manifest in our body," and he now applies that pattern to the transaction between apostle and congregation. His suffering is not merely private discipline; it is fruitful for other people, which is why he can immediately add that "all things are for your sakes." Ministry is thereby described as participation in the shape of the cross — costly at the point of delivery, life-giving at the point of reception — and the whole exchange terminates not in the minister's reputation but in "the thanksgiving of many" redounding "to the glory of God."

The final weighing is deliberately outrageous, and its terms should not be softened. "Our light affliction, which is but for a moment" is written by a man being killed by inches; "a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" is the counterweight, and the verb between them is active — affliction "worketh" the glory rather than merely preceding it. Two clocks are running simultaneously in the same person, since "though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day," and only one of them is visible. That is why the chapter ends with a rule of attention rather than a rule of feeling: "While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen." The visible is not denied; it is dated. "The things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal."

crossRefs.label: Genesis 1:3 — And God said, Let there be light: and there was light
crossRefs.why: Paul's "God, who commanded the light to shine out of darkness, hath shined in our hearts" reaches back to the first day of creation and makes conversion an act of the same order. Reading the source shows what the parallel claims: the darkness is not consulted, the light is spoken into being, and what results is a new order rather than an improvement of the old. It also explains the chapter's confidence in the face of the blinded minds of verse four, since the God who overcame that first darkness is the one now shining.

crossRefs.label: Judges 7:20 — And the three companies blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers, and held the lamps in their left hands
crossRefs.why: Gideon's men hide burning lamps inside clay pitchers and the light is only released when the pitchers are smashed, in a battle deliberately reduced to three hundred men so that Israel could not say "Mine own hand hath saved me." The episode is the working picture behind "we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us," and behind the antitheses that follow: the breaking of the container is not the defeat of the mission but the mechanism of it.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 34:33 — And till Moses had done speaking with them, he put a vail on his face
crossRefs.why: The veiled, fading brightness on Moses' face is the background Paul has been working with since the previous chapter, and it sharpens two phrases here. "The light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" answers Moses' face with a face that does not fade and is not veiled, and the blinding of verse four is the tragic inversion of Israel's veil — a covering now placed over minds rather than over glory.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 116:10 — I believed, therefore have I spoken: I was greatly afflicted
crossRefs.why: Verse thirteen quotes this psalm directly, and the psalm's own setting is the point: the speaker is surrounded by "the sorrows of death," is "greatly afflicted," and speaks anyway because he believes. Paul claims "the same spirit of faith" as that sufferer, which shows that his continued preaching under lethal pressure is not novel apostolic heroism but the ordinary logic of faith under affliction, already sung by Israel long before.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 6:10 — Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes
crossRefs.why: Isaiah is commissioned to a people who will hear and not understand, and told so in advance. Set beside "if our gospel be hid, it is hid to them that are lost," the passage supplies the prophetic precedent for a true message that meets closed eyes, and it frames the difficult question this chapter raises about who does the blinding and by what permission. It also models Isaiah's response — he keeps speaking anyway, which is exactly the posture of verse thirteen.

crossRefs.label: Romans 8:18 — the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us
crossRefs.why: Paul performs the identical weighing there, with the same conclusion and a fuller account of the mechanism: creation groans, believers groan, and hope is by definition directed at what is not seen, "for what a man seeth, why doth he yet hope for?" That last point is the argumentative twin of "we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen," and it prevents the verse from being read as denial of the visible rather than as the ordinary structure of hope.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 12:9 — My strength is made perfect in weakness
crossRefs.why: The earthen-vessel principle is worked out there in Paul's own case, with a specific unrelieved affliction and a direct answer from the Lord refusing to remove it. The later chapter supplies what this one asserts: the weakness is not merely tolerated but assigned, and the correct response is to "glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me." Read together, the two passages block any attempt to treat the cracked vessel as a temporary phase to be outgrown.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us" as a statement about how God ordinarily works: through real, weak, material instruments that nonetheless truly carry what they are given. The verse is read as fitting the whole sacramental economy, in which water, oil, bread, wine, and manifestly imperfect ministers are the appointed vessels of a grace that remains entirely God's. It is also read as securing the objectivity of the ministry against the minister's unworthiness — since the power is "of God, and not of us," the treasure is not diminished when the vessel is cracked or even sinful, which is why the effectiveness of the gospel and the sacraments does not rest on the holiness of the one administering them.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters generally read the treasure as the gospel itself, or the knowledge of God's glory named in the preceding verse, and take the contrast as primarily apologetic rather than sacramental: Paul is defending an unimpressive apostolate against rivals who traded on presence and polish. On this reading the verse is a standing rebuke to any ministry that borrows credibility from the container — including impressive institutional or clerical apparatus — and it locates the power in the word preached rather than in an office or a rite. Reformed writers often press the purpose clause hard: God arranges the weakness precisely so that nothing human can be credited. Both traditions agree that Paul is denying that the vessel contributes any of the power, and both apply the verse against personality-driven ministry.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not," Catholic interpretation identifies the blinding agent as Satan rather than God, and reads the blinding as permitted rather than decreed. Because the gospel is genuinely offered to all and Christ died for all, the note takes the blindness as something inflicted upon a resistance that is already culpably present — the previous clause has already called them "them that are lost" — so that Satan's work exploits and confirms a refusal rather than creating an inability for which the person bears no responsibility. Human freedom is preserved on this reading: grace is offered sufficiently, the will can consent or refuse, and the tradition further allows that some who do not believe are hindered by ignorance for which they are not fully answerable.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed interpreters read verses four and six as a matched pair describing bondage and its only remedy: the mind is blinded and therefore cannot see, and what changes that is not persuasion or a cooperating decision but God commanding light out of darkness in the heart, the same creative fiat as Genesis. On this reading the passage is a strong witness to the necessity of effectual, sovereign grace, and Satan's agency operates within God's overruling purpose rather than as a rival power. Arminian and Wesleyan Protestants stand much closer to the Catholic reading, holding that prevenient grace restores a genuine capacity to respond and that the blinding is resistible. All sides agree the blinding is diabolical rather than divine in origin, and that no evangelistic technique can lift it.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading gives full weight to the active verb in "our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory." Suffering endured in Christ is understood to be genuinely fruitful rather than merely preceding a reward: united to Christ's passion by grace, the believer's affliction really produces something, and this is one of the texts underlying the conviction that the good works and sufferings of those in a state of grace are meritorious — a merit that is itself God's gift, since the whole capacity to suffer fruitfully comes from the grace that makes the union possible. Verse twelve is read in the same key: when Paul says "death worketh in us, but life in you," he affirms that one member's suffering can be salvific in effect for others, which is the scriptural root of offering one's afflictions for the Church.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters accept that affliction is instrumental — God appoints it as the means by which he prepares his people for glory — but resist reading "worketh" as establishing merit. They point to the deliberate disproportion in Paul's own language: a "light" and momentary affliction set against a "far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory" is an incommensurable exchange, which is the logic of grace rather than of wages, and Paul elsewhere insists that present sufferings are "not worthy to be compared" with what is coming. On the vicarious note in verse twelve, Protestants read it as apostolic cost producing benefit through the ministry of the word — Paul's hardships are how the gospel reached Corinth — not as a transferable treasury of satisfaction. Both traditions affirm that Christian suffering is purposeful, not absurd, and that its outcome is secured by God.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads "though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day" as describing a real, progressive interior transformation wrought by grace, not merely a change of legal standing or a shift in perspective. The renewal is daily, cooperative, and cumulative — grace actually remaking the person over time — which fits the broader conviction that sanctification is a genuine healing and elevation of the soul in which the believer participates. The tradition is also careful to deny that the contrast is a body-soul dualism in which the flesh is disposable: verse fourteen has already promised that God "shall raise up us also by Jesus," so the outward man that perishes is destined for resurrection, not for abandonment.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings agree that a real, progressive inward renewal is described and that it is the Spirit's ongoing work, but insist on distinguishing it sharply from justification, which is complete, forensic, and not renewed day by day. Lutheran interpreters often add that the believer remains simultaneously righteous in Christ and a sinner in himself, so the daily renewal never becomes a ground of confidence before God; Reformed writers connect the verse to progressive sanctification as the necessary fruit rather than the basis of acceptance. Protestants likewise reject any dualist reading of outward and inward, appealing to the same resurrection promise in verse fourteen. Both traditions read the verse as the answer to visible decline: what is happening invisibly is running in the opposite direction from what is happening visibly.

verses.text: For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
For in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven:
If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked.
For we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life.
Now he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit.
Therefore we are always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord:
( For we walk by faith, not by sight:)
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him.
For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad.
Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men; but we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences.
For we commend not ourselves again unto you, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf, that ye may have somewhat to answer them which glory in appearance, and not in heart.
For whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God: or whether we be sober, it is for your cause.
For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead:
And that he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again.
Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more.
Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.
And all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation;
To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation.
Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ’s stead, be ye reconciled to God.
For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.

chapters.summary: Paul begins not with a hope but with a claim to knowledge: "For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens." The metaphors shift under his hand — the body is first a tent that can be struck and then a garment, since "in this we groan, earnestly desiring to be clothed upon with our house which is from heaven: If so be that being clothed we shall not be found naked." He is careful to say what the groaning is and is not: "we that are in this tabernacle do groan, being burdened: not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life." The longing is for more embodiment rather than for escape from it, and its guarantee is neither temperament nor argument but a divine deposit already paid: "he that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit." From that pledge follows a settled disposition — "Therefore we are always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord" — qualified by a parenthesis that governs the whole chapter, "( For we walk by faith, not by sight:)." Paul then states the preference plainly: "We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord." Confidence does not dissolve responsibility, because the very next clause is ambition: "Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad." Judgment is what makes his preaching urgent — "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men" — and also what makes self-defence unnecessary, since "we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences." He insists the point is not self-promotion: "we commend not ourselves again unto you, but give you occasion to glory on our behalf, that ye may have somewhat to answer them which glory in appearance, and not in heart," and he hands both extremes of his reputation over to God and to the church — "whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God: or whether we be sober, it is for your cause." Then he names the engine of the whole ministry: "For the love of Christ constraineth us; because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead: And that he died for all, that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again." A death that comprehensive resets perception itself — "Wherefore henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more" — and issues in the chapter's most quoted sentence: "Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new." The initiative is God's from beginning to end, for "all things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ, and hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation; To wit, that God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them; and hath committed unto us the word of reconciliation." That commission gives Paul his standing and his tone at once: "Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God." And the ground of the whole appeal is set down in a single sentence of exchange that the chapter does not explain but simply states: "For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him."
takeaways: Paul's imagery is deliberately unstable and the instability is the argument. A tent "dissolved" would leave a person exposed, so he switches to clothing and then refuses the natural conclusion of his own metaphor: "not for that we would be unclothed, but clothed upon, that mortality might be swallowed up of life." The hope is not that the soul should shed the body but that the mortal body should be overwhelmed by life, the way a garment is put on over another rather than stripped away. This is why the anxiety of being "found naked" appears at all — Paul is not describing liberation from matter but the dread of an unfinished state, and he answers it with a fuller embodiment rather than with a purer spirituality.

The confidence of this chapter is not a mood but an inference from a deposit. "He that hath wrought us for the selfsame thing is God, who also hath given unto us the earnest of the Spirit" — the word describes a first instalment that both guarantees and partially constitutes what is still owed. God has already manufactured the believer for this very outcome and has already paid something down. The parenthesis "( For we walk by faith, not by sight:)" then tells us what kind of knowing sustains the "we know" of the first verse: nothing in the present situation looks like an eternal house, and the certainty does not come from looking.

Assurance and accountability are stated in consecutive breaths without any sense of contradiction. The same apostle who is "always confident" and "willing rather to be absent from the body" says in the next line, "Wherefore we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ." The judgment is universal ("we must all"), individual ("every one"), embodied ("the things done in his body"), and two-sided ("whether it be good or bad"). Paul draws no comfort from vagueness here; instead the prospect fuels his work — "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men" — so that fear of God becomes evangelistic energy rather than paralysis.

The chapter contains a quiet theory of how people should be evaluated. Paul's rivals "glory in appearance, and not in heart," and his defence is not a better display but an appeal to what is already visible to God and, he hopes, to conscience: "we are made manifest unto God; and I trust also are made manifest in your consciences." He then generalizes the principle to the point of scandal — "henceforth know we no man after the flesh: yea, though we have known Christ after the flesh, yet now henceforth know we him no more." If even Christ is no longer assessed by outward impressiveness, then no apostle, and no member of the congregation, may be ranked that way either.

"For the love of Christ constraineth us" is followed immediately by a piece of reasoning, not by a sentiment: "because we thus judge, that if one died for all, then were all dead." The death of the one is read backwards as a diagnosis of the condition of the many; the scope of the remedy discloses the scope of the disease. And the stated purpose of that death is not merely acquittal but a reversal of the direction of a life: "that they which live should not henceforth live unto themselves, but unto him which died for them, and rose again." The verb "constraineth" carries the sense of being hemmed in and pressed forward at once, which is exactly how Paul describes a ministry he did not choose and cannot lay down.

The reconciliation passage keeps the initiative entirely with God while ending in a plea. "All things are of God, who hath reconciled us to himself by Jesus Christ" — the offended party acts, the offender is acted upon, and "God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them." Yet what God has accomplished is then "committed unto us" as a "word," and delivered by "ambassadors for Christ" who speak "in Christ's stead," so that the divine appeal reaches people through human speech. Most striking of all, the plea "be ye reconciled to God" is addressed to a baptized congregation, which means Paul does not treat reconciliation as a transaction filed away in the past but as something a church can drift out of and must keep entering.

crossRefs.label: Genesis 3 — they knew that they were naked; unto Adam also and to his wife did the LORD God make coats of skins, and clothed them
crossRefs.why: Paul's odd fear that we should "be found naked" and his preference to be "clothed upon" reach back to the first consequence of sin, where nakedness is exposure and shame rather than mere bodilessness, and where God himself supplies the covering the guilty could not make for themselves. Read together, the chapter's clothing language becomes the reversal of Eden: the covering God provides at the end is not skins over shame but life over mortality.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 53 — the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all; thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin
crossRefs.why: The final verse of the chapter, "he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin," is unintelligible without the servant song, which supplies both halves of the paradox: a sufferer in whom is no violence or deceit, and a sufferer treated as bearing the iniquity of others. Isaiah's phrase "an offering for sin" also explains the strange grammar of "made him to be sin," since in the sacrificial idiom the same word can name both the offence and the offering that answers it.

crossRefs.label: Romans 5 — when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son
crossRefs.why: Paul argues at length there what he compresses here into three verses: that reconciliation is unilateral in origin, accomplished while the parties were hostile, and grounded in a death offered on behalf of the ungodly. The parallel clarifies the direction of the transaction in "God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself" — it is never God who is talked round, but the estranged who are brought back, which is why the ambassadors' plea can only be "be ye reconciled to God."

crossRefs.label: Romans 14:10-12 — we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ... every one of us shall give account of himself to God
crossRefs.why: The nearest verbal parallel to "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ," and its context is decisive for how the image should be used. There the certainty of universal judgment is the reason to stop judging one another, since none of us lives or dies to himself. Set beside this chapter, the same tribunal that presses Paul to "persuade men" also disqualifies the Corinthians' habit of ranking their teachers by appearance.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 15 — this mortal must put on immortality... Death is swallowed up in victory
crossRefs.why: The two chapters share a vocabulary that is unmistakable: putting on, mortality, and being swallowed up. What Paul states here as a personal longing he had already argued there as doctrine, describing a body sown in corruption and raised in incorruption. Reading them together prevents "absent from the body" from being taken as the goal of Christian hope, since the same author locates the goal in a raised and transformed body rather than in a permanent separation.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 1:23 — having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better
crossRefs.why: This is the closest thing Paul writes to a commentary on "willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord," and it makes the same movement: a genuine preference for immediate nearness to Christ at death, held in tension with the usefulness of remaining in the flesh for the sake of a congregation. Any account of the state between death and resurrection has to reckon with both passages together, since each assumes the departed are with Christ and neither treats that state as the final hope.

crossRefs.label: Revelation 21 — the tabernacle of God is with men... Behold, I make all things new
crossRefs.why: Two of this chapter's central images arrive at their destination there. The "tabernacle" that here is a fragile body destined for dissolution becomes God's own dwelling permanently pitched among his people, and Paul's "behold, all things are become new" is spoken from the throne over the whole creation. The pairing suggests that the new creation of the individual "in Christ" is not a private renovation but the first instance of something cosmic in scope.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord" and "willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord," the Catholic reading takes Paul to affirm a real and conscious intermediate state: the soul survives the dissolution of "our earthly house of this tabernacle" and is genuinely with Christ, while still awaiting the resurrection of the body that alone answers the desire to be "clothed upon." The chapter is therefore read as holding two things together that are often separated — the blessedness of the departed and the incompleteness of a soul without its body — which is why Paul refuses to describe his hope as being "unclothed." Catholic interpretation also finds in the anxiety of not being "found naked" a natural setting for the conviction that some who die in God's friendship are not yet fit for the vision of God and undergo a purification before it, since Paul plainly expects the state after death to be one of accountability as well as of nearness.

counterpoint.summary: Most Protestant interpreters agree fully with the first half of this reading — the believer who dies is consciously present with the Lord, and the resurrection body remains the final hope — and read "absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord" as one of the clearest scriptural warrants for it. They resist the second half, holding that nothing in the passage speaks of a purifying interval, and that Paul's expectation of immediate presence and his confidence "always" would be strained by one; on their reading the believer's fitness for God's presence is not achieved between death and glory but given in Christ. A minority Protestant tradition reads the interval instead as an unconscious sleep until the resurrection, taking Paul's real interest to be the transition itself rather than any duration. All sides note that Paul's stated preference is not for disembodiment as such but for nearness to Christ.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads "we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad" as a genuine judgment of the Christian's works, with real consequences, and as one of the plainest texts against the idea that a believer's deeds are irrelevant to his standing at the end. The preceding verse supplies the corresponding motive: "we labour, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of him." On this reading the good works of the justified are truly the person's own and truly meritorious, though only because they are done in grace and in Christ, so that judgment according to works and salvation by grace are not rivals. Paul's own reaction — "Knowing therefore the terror of the Lord, we persuade men" — is taken as evidence that a healthy fear of God belongs to the Christian life rather than being displaced by assurance.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings agree the judgment is real, universal, and according to works, but distinguish its function. Justification, on this view, is settled already and is not what stands in question at this tribunal; what is assessed is the believer's service, with reward gained or lost while the person is saved. Works are read as the necessary evidence of a living faith rather than as a contribution to acceptance, so that "we may be accepted of him" describes pleasing a Father whose verdict is already favourable in Christ. Interpreters also point to "whether it be good or bad" as ruling out any complacency, and note that the same Paul who writes this chapter grounds confidence at judgment in Christ's death rather than in the believer's record. Both traditions reject the notion that grace makes conduct a matter of indifference.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him," Catholic interpretation stresses the sacrificial idiom behind the phrase: Christ is made a sin offering, identified with the sin he did not commit in order to bear it away, without God regarding the sinless one as personally guilty or turning against him in anger. The second half is read as a real change in us rather than a legal reckoning only — we are "made" the righteousness of God, and made it "in him," that is, by an actual union with Christ in which his righteousness becomes genuinely ours and transforms us. The chapter's own context supports the transformative reading, since the verse follows "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away."

counterpoint.summary: Classical Reformation readings take this verse as the clearest statement of a double exchange in which our sin is reckoned to Christ and his righteousness reckoned to us, received by faith and never at any point a quality we produce. The deliberate symmetry of the sentence is pressed: as Christ was made sin without becoming a sinner, so we are made righteousness without that righteousness originating in us, which is why it is called "the righteousness of God" and located wholly "in him." Many Protestant interpreters additionally read the verse as penal in character, with the penalty due to sin borne in the sinner's place. Others, including some within the tradition, prefer the sin-offering reading and emphasize union with Christ over a purely forensic transfer. All agree the verse gives no ground for boasting and that the exchange is entirely God's doing.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading hears in "hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation" and "we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead" a genuinely representative office, not merely an enthusiastic announcement. An ambassador speaks with the authority of the one who sent him, and Paul says God's own appeal comes through human agents, which Catholic interpretation takes as a pattern for the Church's ordained ministry and for the conviction that God ordinarily reconciles sinners through instruments he has commissioned. That a reconciled congregation is still told "be ye reconciled to God" is read as showing that reconciliation must be continually received after baptism, and as fitting with a sacramental ministry of reconciliation exercised in the Church for sins committed afterward.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters emphasize that what is committed to the apostles is specified in the text itself as a "word" — the message of what God has already done in Christ — so the ambassadorial role is one of proclamation rather than of dispensing reconciliation. On this view every Christian bears the message and the minister's authority is derivative from the gospel he announces, not from a priestly capacity to mediate. The plea to a converted congregation is read as an appeal to live out and hold fast a reconciliation already accomplished, and as evidence that the gospel is preached to the church as well as to the world. Both traditions agree the reconciliation itself is God's act, that the appeal is God's own appeal, and that it reaches its hearers through commissioned human speech.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new," Catholic interpretation reads the newness as an objective, ontological change effected by incorporation into Christ, ordinarily begun in baptism, in which the person is really made new and not merely regarded as new or newly motivated. The immediately preceding verse governs it: because "one died for all, then were all dead," the new creature exists on the far side of a death, so the change is neither self-generated nor gradual in its origin. At the same time this newness is understood as something that must be lived into and can be damaged or lost, which is why the same chapter can address the new creation and still plead "be ye reconciled to God" and warn of a judgment "whether it be good or bad."

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings likewise take the newness as real and God-wrought rather than a change of outlook, and many press the phrase further than an individual reference allows, translating the sense as new creation itself breaking in, so that the verse describes the arrival of a new order to which the believer now belongs. The context in verse sixteen, where perception "after the flesh" is abandoned, is read as supporting this cosmic sense. On the question of loss, Reformed interpreters hold that a genuine new creation cannot be undone, since the change is God's work and the Spirit given is an "earnest"; Arminian and Wesleyan Protestants agree with the Catholic caution that the gift can be forfeited by unbelief. Both traditions read the verse as excluding any account of conversion that leaves a person essentially unchanged.

verses.text: We then, as workers together with him, beseech you also that ye receive not the grace of God in vain.
( For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee: behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation.)
Giving no offence in any thing, that the ministry be not blamed:
But in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God, in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses,
In stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings;
By pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness, by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned,
By the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left,
By honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report: as deceivers, and yet true;
As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed;
As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things.
O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged.
Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels.
Now for a recompence in the same, (I speak as unto my children,) be ye also enlarged.
Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers: for what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness?
And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?

And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? for ye are the temple of the living God; as God hath said, I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you,
And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty.

chapters.summary: Having just described himself as an ambassador begging on Christ's behalf, Paul now names the partnership and the peril together: "We then, as workers together with him, beseech you also that ye receive not the grace of God in vain." The warning is addressed not to outsiders but to a congregation that has already received grace, and it assumes that grace can be received and still come to nothing. To press the urgency he reaches for an oracle of divine answer — "For he saith, I have heard thee in a time accepted, and in the day of salvation have I succoured thee" — and then breaks in with his own doubled exclamation, transposing the prophecy into the present: "behold, now is the accepted time; behold, now is the day of salvation." What follows is Paul's defence of his own ministry, offered not as self-praise but as evidence, and it begins with a negative concern for the office rather than the man: "Giving no offence in any thing, that the ministry be not blamed: But in all things approving ourselves as the ministers of God." The credentials come in a long, accelerating list that shifts preposition twice. First the circumstances endured — "in much patience, in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, In stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults, in labours, in watchings, in fastings" — nine hardships, three of them inflicted by hostile power and three of them self-imposed. Then the resources by which they are borne: "By pureness, by knowledge, by longsuffering, by kindness, by the Holy Ghost, by love unfeigned, By the word of truth, by the power of God, by the armour of righteousness on the right hand and on the left." Then the reception, which is double-edged from the start — "By honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report" — and this tips the list into a series of paradoxes in which the world's verdict and God's are set side by side: "as deceivers, and yet true; As unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and, behold, we live; as chastened, and not killed; As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things." The argument then turns suddenly personal, and Paul does something he does nowhere else in this letter — he calls them by name. "O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged." The diagnosis that follows locates the blockage precisely: "Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels," and the only payment he asks for is symmetry of affection, requested in a father's voice: "Now for a recompence in the same, (I speak as unto my children,) be ye also enlarged." From that plea for an opened heart Paul moves without transition to a demand for a closed door: "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers." Five rhetorical questions follow, each pairing two things that cannot be made one — "what fellowship hath righteousness with unrighteousness? and what communion hath light with darkness? And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel? And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols?" — and the fifth question does not end in a prohibition but in an identity: "for ye are the temple of the living God." That identity is then established out of Scripture itself, a chain of promises stitched into one divine speech: "I will dwell in them, and walk in them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people. Wherefore come out from among them, and be ye separate, saith the Lord, and touch not the unclean thing; and I will receive you, And will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters, saith the Lord Almighty." The chapter that opened with a warning about grace received in vain closes with the reason such grace must not be squandered: the people warned are the dwelling place of God and the adopted children of the Almighty.
takeaways: The chapter opens by holding two things together that are often separated: God's initiative and the real possibility of human waste. Paul and his colleagues are "workers together with him," and the very next clause is the fear that the Corinthians might "receive not the grace of God in vain." The warning presupposes that grace has already been given — this is not an appeal to the unconverted — and that a gift genuinely received can still be rendered fruitless by the one who holds it. Paul then refuses to let the matter be postponed. He takes a prophetic word spoken to God's servant in the past tense, "I have heard thee in a time accepted," and cracks it open with a twice-repeated "behold" that drags it into the present: "now is the accepted time; now is the day of salvation." Prophecy is not treated as a prediction awaiting fulfilment somewhere ahead, but as a window that has opened onto the hearer's own morning.

The credential list is built with a deliberate grammatical architecture that most readings flatten. The first movement is governed by "in" and names circumstances suffered — "in afflictions, in necessities, in distresses, In stripes, in imprisonments, in tumults" — with the last three, "in labours, in watchings, in fastings," quietly shifting from what was done to Paul to what Paul did to himself. The second movement is governed by "by" and names the equipment: moral qualities first, "pureness, knowledge, longsuffering, kindness," then the divine agents, "the Holy Ghost," "the word of truth," "the power of God." The third movement collapses into paradox. Read in sequence, the list argues that a ministry is authenticated neither by its comfort nor by its results but by the coherence of endurance, character, and divine power under conditions that would expose a fraud.

"By honour and dishonour, by evil report and good report" is the hinge on which the whole catalogue turns, because it concedes that Paul's reputation is genuinely mixed and then declines to treat that as a problem. The paradoxes that follow are not consolations offered to a defeated man; they are a systematic refusal of the Corinthian habit of judging ministers by appearance. "As deceivers, and yet true" grants the accusation as a perception while denying it as a fact. "As dying, and, behold, we live" places the same "behold" here that announced the day of salvation, so that the apostle's survival is itself a sign of the accepted time. And "as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things" describes a wealth that can only be measured by what it transfers to others, which is precisely the wealth a status-conscious congregation was least equipped to recognize.

The three verses at the centre are the emotional pivot of the letter, and they are unusually raw. Paul names the church directly — "O ye Corinthians" — something he does only when the pressure is greatest, and describes an openness that is both verbal and affective: "our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged." Then he places the fault where it belongs: "Ye are not straitened in us, but ye are straitened in your own bowels." The constriction is theirs, not his. What he asks in return is not money, not obedience, not an apology, but the same enlargement, and he asks it in the register of family rather than authority: "(I speak as unto my children,) be ye also enlarged." A heart narrowed toward a faithful pastor and a heart wide open to compromising alliances are, in the argument that follows, the same disorder viewed from two sides.

The command "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers" is argued rather than merely imposed, and its argument is a cascade of five questions that each ask the same thing in a rising key — righteousness and unrighteousness, light and darkness, Christ and Belial, believer and infidel, temple and idols. The progression moves from abstract moral qualities to cosmic opposites to named persons to concrete cultic objects, tightening from principle to practice. Crucially, the series does not terminate in a rule. The fifth question is answered by a declaration of who the Corinthians already are: "for ye are the temple of the living God." Separation is therefore grounded in indwelling rather than in contempt. The reason a Christian cannot be harnessed to idolatry is not that unbelievers are disgusting but that the believer is occupied territory, and God does not share a sanctuary with what displaces him.

The closing promises are a mosaic of Scripture rather than a single quotation, and the seams are where the theology happens. The tabernacle pledge that God would dwell and walk among his people, the summons to leave an unclean land and touch no unclean thing, and the covenant with the house of David are welded into one continuous speech of "the Lord Almighty" and applied to a largely Gentile congregation in a Greek port city. Two moves in that mosaic are striking. First, the dwelling promise is made interior — "I will dwell in them, and walk in them" — so that the temple is the people rather than a building they visit. Second, a promise of sonship originally spoken to one royal heir is pluralized and widened to "my sons and daughters," explicitly including women in an adoption that the older text had reserved to a king. A chapter that began by warning against wasting grace ends by describing how much has actually been given.

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 49:8 — In an acceptable time have I heard thee, and in a day of salvation have I helped thee
crossRefs.why: This is the oracle Paul quotes in verse 2, and its original setting sharpens his point. The words are spoken to a servant who has just complained, "I have laboured in vain, I have spent my strength for nought," and who is answered with a commission enlarged rather than withdrawn. Paul, warning a church against receiving grace "in vain" while listing his own labours, is standing inside that servant's situation, and his added "behold, now" claims that the promised day of help has arrived in Christ and is presently open to the Corinthians.

crossRefs.label: Leviticus 26:11-12 — I will set my tabernacle among you... and I will walk among you, and will be your God, and ye shall be my people
crossRefs.why: The first strand of the catena in verse 16 comes from the covenant blessings of Leviticus, where God's dwelling and walking among Israel is the reward of fidelity and stands immediately alongside the demand that they make no idols. Paul changes the preposition from among to within — "I will dwell in them, and walk in them" — which converts a promise about a sanctuary in the camp into a claim about the congregation itself, and explains why he can move from the temple/idol contrast straight to "ye are the temple of the living God."

crossRefs.label: Isaiah 52:11 — Depart ye, depart ye, go ye out from thence, touch no unclean thing
crossRefs.why: Verse 17's "come out from among them, and be ye separate... and touch not the unclean thing" is drawn from this summons, addressed to those carrying the vessels of the Lord out of Babylon. Reading the source shows that the separation Paul commands is framed as an exodus and as an act of worship rather than as social disdain: the ones told to leave are those who bear holy things, and the departure is toward a restored Zion. It also supplies the note of confidence, since the same passage insists the exiles "shall not go out with haste, nor go by flight."

crossRefs.label: 2 Samuel 7:14 — I will be his father, and he shall be my son
crossRefs.why: The final promise in verse 18 takes the dynastic covenant spoken to David about his heir and turns it plural and inclusive: "I will be a Father unto you, and ye shall be my sons and daughters." The original is also the passage where God declines to be housed in a building and promises instead to build David a house, which is the same reversal Paul performs when he identifies the temple with the people. Set together, the two texts show a royal, exclusive promise being distributed across an entire congregation, women expressly named.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 22:10 — Thou shalt not plow with an ox and an ass together
crossRefs.why: The image behind "unequally yoked" belongs to the laws against mixing kinds — plough teams, seed, and cloth — and the picture is agricultural before it is moral. Two animals of unlike strength and stride harnessed to one plough do not merely offend a rule; they injure each other and cut a crooked furrow. That concreteness guards against reading Paul's command as a general call to shun outsiders, since the law concerns being bound into a single working partnership, not sharing a field or a road.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 5:10 — yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world... for then must ye needs go out of the world
crossRefs.why: Paul had already corrected a Corinthian misreading of exactly this kind of separation language, insisting that he never meant withdrawal from unbelieving society, since that would require leaving the world altogether, and that the discipline in view concerns those inside the church. That earlier clarification is the single most important control on "come out from among them, and be ye separate," and it prevents the verse from being turned into a general programme of social quarantine.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 7:13-14 — let her not leave him. For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife
crossRefs.why: The most obvious application of "unequally yoked" is marriage, and Paul's own ruling complicates the simple version of it. A believer already married to an unbeliever is told to stay, and the direction of contagion is reversed: the unbelieving spouse is sanctified rather than the believing one defiled. Read alongside chapter 6, the two passages distinguish between forming a binding alliance with unbelief and remaining faithfully inside one already formed.

crossRefs.label: 2 Corinthians 11:23-27 — in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequent, in deaths oft
crossRefs.why: Paul returns to the hardship catalogue at far greater length and with open reluctance, calling the exercise foolish boasting forced on him by rivals. The later list names the specific beatings, shipwrecks, and dangers that chapter 6 keeps generic, and it makes the polemical setting explicit: these credentials are offered against opponents whose appeal rested on presence, eloquence, and letters of recommendation. The comparison shows that the paradoxes of "as poor, yet making many rich" are an argument about what authenticates ministry, not a devotional flourish.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "workers together with him" and "that ye receive not the grace of God in vain" as a plain statement that grace, while entirely God's initiative and gift, genuinely enlists and requires the free cooperation of the one who receives it. On this view the warning is real because the outcome is real: a person who has been given grace can fail to let it bear fruit, and the whole apostolic ministry described in this chapter exists as one of the instruments God uses to prevent that failure. The passage is therefore read as evidence against any account of salvation in which the human will is merely passive, and the urgency of "behold, now is the accepted time" is understood as a summons to act within a window that can be missed.

counterpoint.summary: Reformed interpreters generally agree that the warning is serious and that it addresses professing believers, but read it as one of the appointed means by which God preserves those who are truly his, so that the exhortation is effective rather than merely conditional; on this reading, receiving grace "in vain" describes an outward reception of the gospel that was never accompanied by regenerating faith, and the language of co-working refers to Paul and his colleagues labouring alongside God in the ministry, not to a division of credit in salvation itself. Wesleyan and Arminian Protestants read the verse much as Catholics do, holding that grace can be resisted and forfeited. All sides insist the initiative and the power belong to God alone.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads the catalogue of afflictions and the paradoxes of verses 8 to 10 in continuity with the earlier claim that the apostles carry about in the body the dying of the Lord Jesus. Ministerial suffering is not merely the cost of the work but is taken up into it: the pattern "as dying, and, behold, we live" is the paschal shape of Christ himself reproduced in his ministers, and their afflictions have a genuine fruitfulness for the church, since it is precisely "as poor" that they are "making many rich." This grounds the conviction that the sufferings of Christians, joined to Christ's own, are not spiritually inert but are drawn into the way grace reaches others, and it explains why Paul can offer his hardships as credentials rather than as excuses.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readers affirm the cruciform pattern and Paul's identification with Christ's sufferings, but resist any suggestion that ministerial affliction adds to or supplements the atonement, which they hold to be finished and sufficient. On their reading the paradoxes are apologetic and pastoral: Paul is dismantling the Corinthian preference for impressive apostles by showing that divine power is displayed through weakness, and the enrichment of others comes through the gospel he preaches rather than through the value of his pain. Many also stress that the list functions as a test of authenticity available to every believer, not as a special class of merit belonging to office-holders. Both traditions agree that the sufferings are real, are borne "by the power of God," and are meant to benefit the church.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers," Catholic reading understands the prohibition as concerning binding partnerships that would compromise faith and worship — above all participation in idolatrous cult, but also marriage, which is why the Church has historically required a dispensation and safeguards for a Catholic marrying a non-believer while still recognizing such marriages as valid. The five contrasts are read as a warning about the integrity of a life claimed by God, not as a licence for withdrawal from society, since Paul elsewhere expressly denies that meaning and since the same letter presents the apostles as ambassadors sent into the world to reconcile it. Separation, in this reading, is separation from idolatry and from what would sever communion, not separation from unbelievers as persons.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant readings range widely. Anabaptist and separatist traditions have taken the verse as a foundational text for a visibly distinct community that refuses oaths, arms, and entanglement with worldly powers, reading "come out from among them, and be ye separate" as a standing ecclesial mandate. Much conservative evangelical interpretation applies it primarily to marriage and business partnership and, in some quarters, to cooperation with churches judged doctrinally unfaithful. Other Protestant interpreters restrict it narrowly to the immediate Corinthian issue of idol-feasts and the false apostles under attack in this letter, arguing that Paul's own instruction to remain in an existing mixed marriage rules out any general separationist programme. Nearly all agree the passage forbids alliances that compromise allegiance to Christ; the dispute is over how wide the circle of forbidden alliance runs.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "ye are the temple of the living God" corporately before individually: the Old Testament promises of indwelling, exodus, and adoption are applied to the congregation as a body, which is why the chapter can move from a plea for an enlarged heart toward Paul to a demand for separation from idols without changing subject. Both concern the integrity of one visible communion. The catena's assembly of tabernacle, prophetic, and Davidic texts into a single divine utterance addressed to a Gentile church is read as evidence that the Church stands in genuine continuity with Israel as the covenant people, receiving what was promised to them, and that its holiness is a real consecration rather than a metaphor — a temple actually inhabited, whose defilement is therefore a serious matter.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters agree the temple language is corporate here — the pronouns are plural, and the promise is "I will dwell in them" — and many read this as one of the strongest biblical grounds for the priesthood of all believers, since the sanctuary is now the assembled people rather than a consecrated place or a clerical caste. Where they differ is in locating the continuity with Israel in the gospel promise received by faith rather than in an institutional succession, and in stressing that the resulting holiness is the fruit of union with Christ rather than a property conferred by membership. Some also read the adoption language of "sons and daughters" as conditional in form yet secured by God's own oath as "the Lord Almighty." Both traditions read the passage as making the church itself the dwelling place of God and therefore accountable for what it admits.
