verses.text: This is the third time I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established.

I told you before, and foretell you, as if I were present, the second time; and being absent now I write to them which heretofore have sinned, and to all other, that, if I come again, I will not spare:
Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, which to you-ward is not weak, but is mighty in you.
For though he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you.
Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?
But I trust that ye shall know that we are not reprobates.
Now I pray to God that ye do no evil; not that we should appear approved, but that ye should do that which is honest, though we be as reprobates.
For we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth.
For we are glad, when we are weak, and ye are strong: and this also we wish, even your perfection.
Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction.
Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace; and the God of love and peace shall be with you.
Greet one another with an holy kiss.
All the saints salute you.
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen.

chapters.summary: The letter's last chapter opens as a legal notice. "This is the third time I am coming to you. In the mouth of two or three witnesses shall every word be established" — Paul cites the Mosaic rule of evidence, and whether he means his three visits or the witnesses he intends to summon, the effect is to announce that the coming visit will be a hearing rather than a reunion. The warning is repeated in the awkward tenses of a man who has already said this once and is saying it again in advance: "I told you before, and foretell you, as if I were present, the second time; and being absent now I write to them which heretofore have sinned, and to all other, that, if I come again, I will not spare." His reason for the severity is their own demand: "Since ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me, which to you-ward is not weak, but is mighty in you." They have asked him to prove that Christ speaks through him, and he warns them that they may get the demonstration they asked for and not enjoy it. Then, in a single sentence, he grounds the entire quarrel about weakness and power in the cross itself: "though he was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you." The pattern of Christ is the pattern of his minister — weakness that is real, followed by power that is God's and directed toward this congregation. Having been ordered to submit to examination, Paul turns the instrument around: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?" The logic is disarming, because the Corinthians are themselves the evidence of his apostleship, so that any test they pass vindicates him and any test they fail indicts them along with him. He expresses confidence in the outcome — "I trust that ye shall know that we are not reprobates" — and then, remarkably, offers to lose the argument if it would help: "I pray to God that ye do no evil; not that we should appear approved, but that ye should do that which is honest, though we be as reprobates." He would rather be thought a failure and have them do right than be vindicated by their misconduct, which is the practical form of the maxim that follows: "we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth." The same reversal governs verse nine — "we are glad, when we are weak, and ye are strong" — and the goal is named plainly, "this also we wish, even your perfection," a word suggesting repair and completion, the mending of what has been torn. The purpose of the whole letter is then stated outright: "Therefore I write these things being absent, lest being present I should use sharpness, according to the power which the Lord hath given me to edification, and not to destruction." The severity in the pages is spent precisely so that it need not be spent in person, and the authority is defined once more by what it is for. The closing lines fall into a rapid series of imperatives — "Finally, brethren, farewell. Be perfect, be of good comfort, be of one mind, live in peace" — each answering a specific fracture in the church, with a promise attached: "the God of love and peace shall be with you." Then the ordinary greetings, "Greet one another with an holy kiss. All the saints salute you," and finally the fullest benediction in the Pauline letters, given to the most fractious congregation he ever wrote to: "The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost, be with you all. Amen."
takeaways: Paul frames the visit with a rule of evidence rather than a threat of force. Invoking "two or three witnesses" places his coming inside a procedure the Corinthians can recognise and hold him to, which is a considerable concession from a man they have accused of ruling by intimidating letters. Discipline conducted under a known rule cannot be arbitrary, and the citation quietly answers the charge of verse ten in the previous chapter: the apostle who is said to terrify by post is committing himself in advance to the same standards of proof that protect any accused person under the Law. Severity and due process arrive in the same sentence.

Verse four is the theological heart of the letter compressed into two clauses. "He was crucified through weakness, yet he liveth by the power of God" establishes that in the decisive event of the faith, weakness and power were not alternatives but sequence, and Paul then applies the sequence to himself: "we also are weak in him, but we shall live with him by the power of God toward you." This settles the argument that has run since chapter ten. The Corinthians' criterion — a minister should look strong — would have disqualified Christ on Good Friday, and the pattern of the crucified and risen Lord is not an exception to how God works but the template for how his servants are to be recognised.

The reversal in verse five is one of Paul's sharpest moves and is easy to miss because the sentence has been so thoroughly detached from its setting. They have been auditing him; he tells them to audit themselves — "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves" — and the question is not framed as a threat but as an appeal to something they already know, "Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you." The apostle's credentials and the congregation's own standing turn out to be the same fact viewed from two sides, so a church that questions its founder's legitimacy is standing on a branch it is sawing through.

Verse seven is the most generous sentence Paul ever wrote about his own reputation. He prays that they will do no evil "not that we should appear approved, but that ye should do that which is honest, though we be as reprobates" — accepting, hypothetically, permanent disgrace as the price of their integrity. Coming at the end of four chapters of self-defence, it retroactively reframes the whole apologia: he has argued for his standing not because he needs it but because their acceptance of the gospel is bound up with it, and the moment those two can be separated he abandons his own case without hesitation. The maxim that follows, "we can do nothing against the truth, but for the truth," is his explanation: an apostle has no power that can be used against reality.

The word rendered "perfection" in verse nine and "be perfect" in verse eleven carries the sense of setting a broken thing right — mending a net, resetting a bone, restoring what has been dislocated. Read that way, the letter's closing wish is exactly matched to its subject: a congregation fractured by factions, damaged by a painful confrontation, and pulled apart by rival teachers is asked to be put back together. The imperatives that follow are correspondingly specific to the diagnosis — comfort for those wounded by the severe letter, one mind against the parties, peace against the debates and tumults he feared in the previous chapter — and the promise attached names God by the two qualities the church has been short of.

The final benediction is remarkable for where it lands. Paul names Father, Son, and Spirit in one breath, assigning grace to Christ, love to God, and communion to the Holy Ghost, and he pronounces it over the congregation that has caused him more grief than any other. The order is worth noticing, since grace comes first as the point of access and communion last as the result, and the whole is given "to you all" — including, presumably, the party that has been attacking him. Whatever the visit will bring, the letter ends by placing the entire church, unresolved quarrels and all, inside the life of the God whose fellowship it has been failing to reflect.

crossRefs.label: Deuteronomy 19:15 — at the mouth of two witnesses, or at the mouth of three witnesses, shall the matter be established
crossRefs.why: Paul quotes this rule verbatim to open the chapter, and the surrounding legislation shows why it mattered. The law exists to protect the accused from a single hostile voice, and it is immediately followed by severe penalties for the false witness, so the standard cuts against accusers as much as it enables prosecution. Importing it into a church dispute means that the coming discipline will not proceed on rumour, that the accusations circulating about Paul are themselves subject to the rule, and that a congregation which has been trading in "backbitings" and "whisperings" is being told what will and will not be admitted when he arrives.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 18:16-18 — take with thee one or two more; whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound in heaven
crossRefs.why: Jesus applies the same Mosaic rule to disputes within the community, and the procedure he lays out — private approach, then witnesses, then the assembly — is the nearest thing in the gospels to what Paul is preparing to do at Corinth. The passage also supplies the authority behind his warning that he will not spare, since the escalation ends in a decision the church makes and heaven ratifies. Read together, the two texts show discipline understood as a graduated, evidence-bound process whose aim is stated in the first line, "thou hast gained thy brother," which matches Paul's insistence that his power is for edification and not destruction.

crossRefs.label: 1 Corinthians 11:28-31 — let a man examine himself; for if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged
crossRefs.why: This is the same command to self-examination given to the same church, and there it is attached to the Lord's Supper and to a real crisis of unworthy participation. The two passages illuminate each other: the earlier one supplies the concrete setting in which Corinthian Christians were expected to test themselves, and the later one broadens the scope from a single act of communion to the whole question of whether they are "in the faith." The earlier text also supplies the consequence Paul assumes here, that self-judgment forestalls judgment, which explains why he presses them to examine themselves before he arrives to do it for them.

crossRefs.label: Psalm 139:23-24 — search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts
crossRefs.why: The psalm gives the posture that keeps self-examination from collapsing into either complacency or despair, since the examining is finally handed back to the God who already knows the answer. Its request, "see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting," pairs diagnosis with a plea for guidance rather than leaving the searcher alone with his findings. Set beside "examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith," it supplies the assumption Paul is working with: the self is genuinely opaque to itself, so the test is conducted in the presence of one who searches more thoroughly than we can.

crossRefs.label: Romans 8:9-10 — if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his; if Christ be in you, the body is dead because of sin
crossRefs.why: Paul's test in verse five — "how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates" — presupposes the doctrine Romans states directly, that indwelling is the mark of belonging and its absence the mark of not belonging. Romans also supplies what the indwelling produces and therefore what an examination could actually look for: the Spirit bearing witness, the mortifying of the deeds of the body, and the cry of sonship. Without that, verse five is an unanswerable question; with it, the self-examination has content, and the criterion is a life visibly under the Spirit's government rather than a feeling of certainty.

crossRefs.label: Philippians 2:8-9 — he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death; wherefore God also hath highly exalted him
crossRefs.why: The two-stage pattern Paul compresses into verse four — crucified through weakness, living by the power of God — is set out at length here as humiliation followed by exaltation, and it is applied to the readers as the mind they are to have among themselves. That application is exactly what the Corinthians need, since their fault is a preference for strength that shows and a contempt for a minister who looks defeated. Reading the hymn behind 2 Corinthians 13 shows that Paul is not making a special plea for his own case but describing the shape of everything God does in Christ, into which apostles and congregations alike are drawn.

crossRefs.label: Romans 15:5-6 — the God of patience and consolation grant you to be likeminded one toward another
crossRefs.why: The closing imperatives of 2 Corinthians — be of one mind, live in peace — appear in Romans as a prayer rather than a command, and the difference is instructive. Paul asks God to grant the very unity he elsewhere orders, which keeps the exhortation from being merely moral advice addressed to people who have already failed at it. The Romans passage also supplies the goal of such unity, that the church may "with one mind and one mouth glorify God," and the ground of it, that Christ received us, which is the same logic by which Paul can pronounce his final blessing on a congregation still in open dispute with him.

crossRefs.label: Matthew 28:19 — baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost
crossRefs.why: The threefold naming that closes 2 Corinthians is one of the earliest surviving instances of Christians speaking of God in this pattern, and the baptismal formula is its counterpart in the gospel tradition. Neither text argues for the doctrine; both simply assume that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit belong together in a single act of naming, which is evidence of how early and how instinctively the pattern was fixed. Reading them together also connects the letter's last line to the moment each Corinthian entered the church, so that the benediction returns the fractured congregation to the terms on which it was constituted.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic reading takes "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves" as a call to a real and repeatable practice rather than to a single settling of the question. Examination of conscience belongs to the ordinary Christian life, is required before approaching the Eucharist, and finds its completion in the sacrament of penance where what the examination uncovers is confessed and absolved. The verse is read alongside Paul's earlier instruction to the same church about examining oneself before receiving the bread and cup, so that self-scrutiny is understood as habitual, concrete, and ordered toward reconciliation rather than toward introspective certainty. The open possibility that a member might be found wanting — "except ye be reprobates" — is taken seriously: grace can be lost by grave sin, assurance is a confident hope rather than an infallible knowledge of one's final state, and the appropriate response to the examination is repentance rather than either presumption or despair.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters read the same command as a call to test whether one is genuinely a believer at all, and typically toward assurance rather than away from it, since Paul's expectation is plainly that they will pass — Christ is in them unless something has gone very wrong. In the Reformed tradition self-examination looks for the fruits and witness of the Spirit as confirmation of a salvation that God preserves, so a true believer may attain settled assurance while a failed examination reveals that the faith was never genuine. Confession to another Christian may be commended, but forgiveness is sought directly from God and requires no priestly absolution. Both traditions agree that the command is addressed to the whole church, that it concerns something testable rather than a private feeling, and that no one is invited to assume his own standing without looking.

interpretationNotes.claim: On "this also we wish, even your perfection" and the imperative "be perfect," Catholic reading hears the universal call to holiness. The word points to a mending and completing that God actually accomplishes in his people, so that sanctification is a genuine transformation with a real terminus rather than a status held at a distance; growth in charity can go very far in this life, the saints are evidence that it does, and any remaining purification is completed before the soul enters the divine presence. Paul's willingness to command what he has just prayed for indicates that the perfecting is both God's gift and the believer's task, undertaken in grace, which is the ordinary Catholic account of how sanctification works. The chapter's practical shape supports the reading, since what is to be mended is named concretely — comfort, one mind, peace — rather than left as an abstraction.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters usually render the word as restoration or maturity rather than perfection in the strict sense, noting that it describes mending what is broken and that Paul is addressing a divided congregation rather than describing the attainment of sinlessness. The dominant Reformation instinct is that the believer remains simultaneously righteous in Christ and a sinner in himself, so sanctification is real and progressive but never complete in this life, and claims of attained perfection are treated as pastorally dangerous. The Wesleyan strand is a notable exception, reading such texts as genuine promises of a heart perfected in love. Both traditions agree that God is the one who mends, that the command is addressed to a community rather than to isolated individuals, and that the goal is concrete restoration rather than a private spiritual attainment.

interpretationNotes.claim: Catholic interpretation reads verse ten as a compact definition of ecclesiastical authority: a real power, given by the Lord, capable of sharpness, and bounded by its purpose — "to edification, and not to destruction." The tradition finds here the principle that governs the exercise of the keys and of every canonical penalty, namely that discipline in the Church is medicinal, aimed at the recovery of the offender and the health of the body, so that a penalty which cannot serve that end has exceeded the authority it claims. Paul's practice illustrates the principle: he writes in advance precisely so that he will not have to act severely in person, he invokes a rule of evidence, and he would rather forfeit his own vindication than damage them. Authority so understood is genuinely juridical and genuinely constrained, and the constraint comes from the nature of the office rather than from the goodwill of the officeholder.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters affirm the same purpose clause with particular emphasis, frequently citing it as the standing test by which church authority is judged and found wanting whenever discipline becomes punitive or self-protective. The stress falls on the fact that Paul's power is exercised almost entirely through writing, argument, and prayer, and that his final recourse is to hope the congregation will correct itself so that no exercise of authority is needed at all; on this reading the power is ministerial, deriving all its force from the truth it serves, as verse eight says outright. Many add that the authority belongs to the gospel rather than to a jurisdiction that can be inherited. Both traditions agree that the authority is genuinely given by the Lord, that it can be used, and that using it to destroy rather than to build is an abuse rather than an application of it.
